name: Table formats
summary: A metadata layer that turns a folder of data files into a real table, with transactions, schema changes and time travel.
howItWorks: Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake and Apache Hudi keep metadata files next to the Parquet data files. Each commit writes new data files plus a new snapshot listing exactly which files make up the table, then makes it current in one atomic step: swapping a pointer in a catalog (Iceberg) or adding the next entry to a transaction log (Delta Lake). That gives you ACID transactions on object storage. Readers always see a complete snapshot, concurrent writers detect conflicts and retry, and old snapshots stay readable for time travel until you expire them. Adding or renaming a column is a metadata change, so it doesn’t rewrite the data.
analogy: The catalogue of a library whose books never move. The catalogue says which books make up the collection right now, and you can pull last year’s edition to see what it said then.
useWhen: Tables in object storage that several engines, such as Spark, Trino, Snowflake and DuckDB, must read and write safely
Updates, deletes and upserts on lake data, such as erasing a customer or applying change-data capture
Auditing or reproducing a report exactly as of a past snapshot
avoidWhen: Many small single-row writes per second; each commit adds files and metadata, so batch them or use a database
A handful of files that one tool reads; plain Parquet is enough
example: A streaming job commits new orders to an Iceberg table every minute while a nightly job compacts small files and deletes rows for customers who asked to be erased. Analysts in Trino and data scientists in Spark query the same table and never see a half-written commit. Finance reruns last quarter’s report against the snapshot from 1 July.

source: -- Spark SQL with an Iceberg catalog named "lake"
order_id BIGINT, customer_id BIGINT, amount DECIMAL(10,2), ts TIMESTAMP
USING updates u ON t.order_id = u.order_id
-- time travel: the table as it was on 1 July
SELECT sum(amount) FROM lake.sales.orders TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-07-01 00:00:00';

diagram.caption: Two writers commit to one table. The catalog accepts one commit at a time, so a writer that loses a race gets a conflict and retries. Each accepted commit is a new numbered snapshot. Dashboards follow the latest snapshot, while an audit job reads an older one. Snapshots past retention are expired, and the audit skips ahead.

story: Hive, built at Facebook and described in a 2009 VLDB paper, gave Hadoop its idea of a table: an HDFS directory of files, split into partition subdirectories such as `ds=20090101`, with a metastore recording each table’s schema and location. That worked for batch loads, but the files were the truth. Readers found data by listing directories, writers changed tables by adding and renaming files, and nothing stopped a query from seeing half of an update.

Cloud object stores made this worse. Listing millions of objects was slow, consistency guarantees were limited, and a rename on S3 is really a copy. Between 2016 and 2017 three companies built a fix independently: Uber built Hudi to apply database changes to its lake within minutes, Netflix started Iceberg to replace Hive’s layout with a spec that tracks every file, and Databricks launched Delta Lake after cloud storage problems caused around half of its support escalations. All three record the exact list of files in each table version and switch versions atomically.

All three were open source by 2019 and competed for years before converging. Delta’s UniForm (2023) writes Iceberg and Hudi metadata, Apache XTable converts between formats, and in 2024 Databricks agreed to acquire Tabular, the company founded by Iceberg’s creators. Newer designs such as DuckLake (2025) move the metadata into a SQL database altogether.

choices.why: Listing directories is slow on object stores and can’t tell a finished write from a half-written one. A manifest or log that names every file makes the table’s contents exact.

Object stores have no multi-object transactions, but a single small write can be made atomic: swapping a pointer in a catalog (Iceberg) or creating the next log file (Delta Lake). Writers that lose the race retry.

choices.choice: Immutable data files plus delete markers
choices.why: Parquet files can’t be edited in place, so updates write new files, and Iceberg v2 records deleted rows in separate delete files instead of rewriting whole files.
Because files are never modified, an old version costs only storage. That gives time travel and reproducible reads until the snapshot is expired.

timeline.text: Hive paper describes tables as directories plus a metastore
Uber builds Hudi to apply updates to its Hadoop lake
Iceberg starts at Netflix; Databricks launches Delta for customers
Delta Lake open-sourced; Hudi joins Iceberg in the Apache Incubator
Delta Lake UniForm writes Iceberg and Hudi metadata
XTable enters the Apache Incubator; Databricks agrees to buy Tabular
DuckLake keeps table metadata in SQL; Iceberg adds v3 deletion vectors
